capstone.title: Launch week: one pipeline, end to end
capstone.workflow_name: Launch pipeline — sign-ups to CRM and #new-leads
capstone.scene: Friday. Nebula's spring launch goes live on Monday, and Ana wants one pipeline she can trust: every sign-up from the form cleaned, checked, saved to HubSpot and announced to sales. Nothing dirty, nothing doubled, nothing lost without a word. You built each piece in the modules. Now build the whole thing on your own, in the sandbox, and prove it against the launch-day data.

requirements.text: Starts from the Google Sheets Trigger on Launch sign-ups › Form responses: one new row, one run
Cleans every row first: email trimmed and lower-case, name trimmed, plan lower-case (blank becomes "starter"), sign-up date as yyyy-MM-dd
Sends rows with no usable email to the Rejected sign-ups sheet, with the person's name and a reason
Stops repeat sign-ups by comparing cleaned emails, even when the repeat arrives as a separate run
Creates or updates the HubSpot contact for clean, unique rows only: email, full name, plan and sign-up date
Posts to #new-leads only after the HubSpot write, with the person's name, email and plan
Retries when HubSpot is rate-limited, and reports a HubSpot outage in #ops-alerts instead of losing the row
Has a name a teammate would understand, no keys typed into fields, and no loose nodes

edge_cases: The form double-fires: the same person arrives twice, a minute apart, with the email typed differently
Emails come with capitals, spaces and tabs around them
About 8% of rows have no usable email: blank, only spaces, or not an address ("nadia@")
Dates arrive three ways: 2026-03-14, 14/03/2026 and March 14, 2026, sometimes with a time after them
Plan is blank for some people and in capitals (PRO) for others
HubSpot rate-limits bursts (429) and was down for a few minutes during the last launch (503)
capstone.closing: The whole course in one build: a trigger, a cleaning step, two guards, a write, an alert and a plan for when the CRM fails. Expect it to take about an hour. Your work saves as you go.

sheets.name: Form responses
sheets.note: One row per sign-up. New rows arrive while the launch runs.

sheets.name: Rejected sign-ups
sheets.note: Empty. Rows that can't be used go here, with a reason.

channels.name: #new-leads
channels.note: Sales. One message per new contact in HubSpot.

channels.name: #ops-alerts
channels.note: The team that fixes things. Failures go here.

sample.note: HubSpot answers 429 on the first try

real_n8n.intro: Running real n8n (cloud or self-hosted)? The sandbox uses the same nodes and settings, so you can rebuild it there:
steps: Create three credentials in n8n: Google Sheets, HubSpot and Slack.
Add the nodes in the same order. Parameter names match what you set here, and expressions can be copied as they are.
Set Retry On Fail and On Error on the HubSpot node's Settings tab, then connect its error output.
Add a test row to your sheet, click Execute workflow, then Publish.

reactions.text: launch day ran itself. 320 sign-ups in the CRM, 320 alerts, zero junk. i checked five by hand. all clean.
every alert was a real person who was already in the CRM when i clicked. that has never happened before
the form double-fired again and nobody noticed. which i think is the point 🙃

items.stem: Which statement about executions and items is correct?

options.text: Each item starts its own execution, so a node only ever sees one item
One trigger event starts one execution, which can carry many items; each node then runs once per item
An execution only exists once the last node has succeeded
Items are shared between executions until a filter clears them

items.stem: A lead-alert workflow showed green for 61 hours while no alerts arrived. The trigger fired on every new row. Which single check finds the cause fastest?

options.text: Open the last node’s response in a recent run and read what the receiving system returned
Fire the trigger again by hand and watch whether it turns green
Add a Wait node before the alert so the call has more time
Rename the sheet columns so the filter reads them correctly

items.stem: What is the essential difference between a Set node and a Filter node?

options.text: Set runs once per execution; Filter runs once per item
Set removes fields that fail a rule; Filter renames the ones that pass
Set changes what each item looks like and passes every item on; Filter leaves items unchanged and decides which ones continue
They do the same job; Filter is simply the faster of the two

items.stem: 300 rows arrive: 36 have no email and 41 are repeats of leads already seen. Both guards sit before the alert. How many alerts are sent — and how many would be sent if the duplicate guard were moved to after the alert?

options.text: 264 are sent; with the guard moved, 300
223 are sent; with the guard moved, still 223
259 are sent; with the guard moved, 300
223 are sent; with the guard moved, 264

items.stem: Why is “the run is green” not proof that the work was done?

options.text: Green only means the trigger fired; later nodes are not checked
A node reports success when it ran without throwing an error; the receiving system can still have rejected or ignored the call
Green runs are cached, so they may show an older result
Green is shown whenever fewer than half of the items fail

items.stem: After deduplication the CRM still holds one customer twice: “priya@x.com” and “ Priya@X.com”. The duplicate filter is configured correctly. What is the real fault, and the fix?

options.text: The filter is too strict; loosen it to compare names instead of emails
The CRM is at fault; delete the second record by hand after each run
The emails reach the guard un-normalised; trim and lower-case them in a Set node upstream of the filter
The trigger is firing twice; add a Wait node after it

items.stem: When is an expression inside a node evaluated?

options.text: For each item, at the moment that item passes through the node, using that item’s own fields
Once per execution, using the first item only
When the workflow is saved, and the result is stored
Only when the previous node returned an error

items.stem: Some rows have a blank plan; others say “FREE ” with a trailing space. Blanks must default to “free”. Which order avoids ending up with two versions of the same plan?

options.text: Fill the default first, then trim and lower-case
Filter out the blank rows, then fill the default
Fill the default, then filter duplicates, then trim
Trim and lower-case first, then fill the default for whatever is still blank

items.stem: What does “order is the design” mean for guards in a pipeline?

options.text: Guards should be listed alphabetically so reviewers can find them
A guard protects only what comes after it, so it must sit before the action it is meant to protect
The more guards a pipeline has, the safer it is, wherever they sit
Guards belong at the very end, to clean up whatever got through

items.stem: Someone renames the sheet column “Email” to “Contact”. Every run is still green, but every item now stops at the “has an email” filter. Why?

options.text: Renaming a column pauses the trigger until the workflow is re-saved
The filter’s expression still reads the old field name, which is now undefined on every item, so every item fails the condition
Filters stop working when a sheet has more than one text column
The items are being counted as duplicates of each other

items.stem: A pipeline takes in 500 rows and writes 376. Which property makes that result defensible?

options.text: It finished without any error
Most of the rows got through
Each of the 124 stopped rows was stopped by a named guard, and the counts per guard are recorded
The 376 rows were written in the original order

items.stem: You inherit this pipeline: trigger → write to CRM → filter blank emails → Set (normalise) → filter duplicates. What is wrong with it, taken as a whole?

options.text: Only the Set node is misplaced; the two filters are fine where they are
Nothing — the filters still remove the bad rows from the CRM afterwards
The trigger should come last, so that it fires only once
It is back to front: the write happens before any guard, and the guards run before normalisation — it should be normalise, guard, guard, then write

prompts.text: In your own words: why does a pipeline you can trust clean first, guard next, write, and only then alert?
Where did you get stuck in this course, and what helped you get unstuck?
Which task in your own work will you automate first, and which guard will it need?
